title: Research and Writing from Sources
theme: Words for finding, quoting, and citing information
objectives: I can use ten words to talk about finding, quoting, and listing sources.
I can tell the difference between a quotation, an excerpt, and a passage.
I can explain what a footnote, a glossary, and a bibliography are for.
I can plan a short research report and name the tools I would use.
rationale: Fifth graders begin writing from sources, and the words for this work are rarely taught directly. Research, passage, excerpt, quotation, and reference name the sources and what students take from them; highlight names the first move; footnote, glossary, and bibliography name the three tools that make a report checkable. Together the ten words give students a vocabulary for the whole path from question to cited report. The unit follows the argument unit on purpose: a viewpoint needs proof, and proof from a source needs a citation. Students revisit argument, proof, trustworthy, and debate by judging whether a source is reliable and whether a claim is supported. The Ana passage walks through the real steps of a student report so that every word is seen in use.

words.def: To study a topic carefully to find facts and information.
words.ex: We will research the history of our town at the library this week.
words.ex2: Before buying a new bike, Dev decided to research the best brands online.
words.nonExample: Guessing an answer without looking anything up is not research.

apps.academic: Scientists research a question by gathering evidence and testing ideas.
apps.spoken: I need to research my family tree.
apps.writing: Use research as a verb when you study a topic carefully before you write.

passage.title: Ana's Bee Report
paras: Ana had one week to write a report on honeybees, so she began to research at the library. She did not trust the first website she found, because it listed no author and no date. Instead, she asked the librarian for a reference book and a magazine article by a beekeeper. "A good source tells you who wrote it," the librarian said.

At her desk, Ana read one long passage about how bees make honey from nectar. She used a yellow marker to highlight the sentences she might need. One excerpt, a few lines from the beekeeper's article, explained that every colony has one queen. Ana wanted to use the exact words, so she copied them inside quotation marks.

While writing, she added a footnote at the bottom of the page to show where the idea came from. Her readers could look down and see the source at once. She also checked the glossary at the back of her book to make sure she understood the word nectar, and she built a small glossary for her own report.

Last, Ana built a bibliography that listed every book, article, and document she had used, in alphabetical order by the author's last name. One document was the town's beekeeping permit. "Now anyone can check my facts," she said. Mr. Lin read the report and smiled. "You gave me proof for every claim," he said.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "excerpt" most nearly means
choices: a short piece taken from a longer text
a long report written by a student
a list of words and their meanings
a drawing of a bee
qs.why: The text describes a few lines from the beekeeper's article, which is a short piece taken from a longer work.

qs.q: Why did Ana not trust the first website she found?
choices: It had too many pictures.
It was written for children.
It listed no author and no date.
It did not mention bees.
qs.why: The paragraph says the site listed no author and no date, so she could not tell who wrote it or when.

qs.q: Why did Ana put the sentence about the queen inside quotation marks?
choices: She wanted to show she was using the author's exact words.
She wanted the sentence to look bigger.
She could not understand the sentence.
She was afraid it was wrong.
qs.why: The passage says Ana wanted to use the exact words, so she copied them inside quotation marks.

qs.q: What is the main job of Ana's footnote?
choices: It makes the page look neat.
It shows readers where an idea came from.
It explains a hard word.
It lists every book she read.
qs.why: The footnote sits at the bottom of the page to show where the idea came from, so readers can see the source at once.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Bees are the most important insects.
Libraries are better than websites.
A good report keeps track of its sources so that readers can check the facts.
A student should only use one source.
qs.why: Ana researches carefully, quotes exactly, and cites sources so that anyone can check her facts, and the teacher praises her proof.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for finding, taking from, and citing sources: research, reference, and highlight for the work itself; passage, excerpt, quotation, and document for what is read or taken; and footnote, glossary, and bibliography for tools that make a report checkable. The passage is a narrative about a student writing a report, so students see each step in order. The unit follows argument and proof, linking evidence to citation.

notes.va.research.v: Research is a verb here: to study a topic to find facts. The noun is also research. Students may think research means only searching online; broaden to books, interviews, and observation. Model asking a question and listing places to look.
notes.va.passage.n: Passage means a short section of a longer text, and it also means a way through, as in a narrow passageway. Teach the text sense and mention that students will see passage on reading tests. Practice marking a passage with line numbers.
notes.va.excerpt.n: An excerpt is a short selection taken from a longer work. Contrast with quotation: an excerpt may be several lines, while a quotation is the exact words of a person or writer, often a single sentence. Have students excerpt a paragraph from a book.
notes.va.quotation.n: A quotation is exact words, and it needs quotation marks and a source. Students often paraphrase and keep the quotation marks, which changes the meaning. Teach that every word inside the marks must match the source. Note that quote is also a verb.
notes.va.reference.n: Reference as a noun means a source of facts, such as an encyclopedia, or a mention of something. Teach the source sense and mention that we make a reference to something when we mention it. Have students list reference books in the library.
notes.va.document.n: A document is a written or printed paper that gives information or serves as a record, such as a letter, a form, or a certificate. Digital files count too. Students may think a document is only a word-processing file. Ask what documents they see at school.
notes.va.highlight.v: Highlight is a verb that means mark important words with color. Students over-highlight, so teach to mark only key words, not whole pages. Note that highlight is also a noun meaning the best part, but keep the taught verb sense.
notes.va.glossary.n: A glossary lists hard words and meanings, usually at the end of a book. It is like a mini dictionary for that book. Students often confuse a glossary with an index, which lists topics and page numbers. Have students use a glossary to look up a word.
notes.va.footnote.n: A footnote is a short note at the bottom of a page that gives a source or an explanation. Students may confuse it with an endnote, which comes at the end. Point to a footnote in a nonfiction book and read it together.
notes.va.bibliography.n: A bibliography lists the books and sources used to write a report, often in alphabetical order. Students may think it is a list of books they might read someday; it lists the sources they actually used. Show a model entry for a book and a website.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Ana copies the beekeeper's exact words inside quotation marks. That is a quotation. If she had put the idea in her own words, she would not need the marks, but she still needs a footnote to show where the idea came from. I can check by asking whether the words are exact.'
discuss: How is a footnote different from a bibliography, and why might a report need both?
Which source would you trust more for a report on bees, a beekeeper's article or a website with no author, and why?
misconceptions: A quotation can be changed a little and still have quotation marks.
A glossary and an index are the same.
Highlighting a whole page counts as studying it.
A bibliography lists books you want to read.
Research only means searching the internet.
extend: Build a model bibliography entry for a book, a website, and an interview.
Collect five excerpts from different texts and sort them by genre.
Write a one-paragraph report with one quotation, one footnote, and a glossary of two words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit argument, proof, trustworthy, and debate by asking students to judge two sources for a claim, to say which is more trustworthy, and to use a quotation as proof in a short debate turn. Return to the ten words after two days, again at one week, in a real research task.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: cita (quotation), resaltar (highlight; subrayar is also common), nota al pie (footnote), investigar (research), pasaje (passage; fragmento is also common).
Alphabetical order by author's last name is the common convention for a bibliography, but formats vary by style guide.
Honeybee facts in the passage (bees make honey from nectar; a colony has one queen) are standard and widely taught but have not been checked against a cited source. The report scenario is invented.
